### 3.10 The four vocabularies, judged

1. **Adapter kinds (`WorkspaceError`, 10 values).** Partly designed. The id kinds (`InvalidId`, `MissingObject`, `StaleId`) describe the id model that the native shell needs. They are pinned by `tests/workspace/test_workspace_contract.cpp` and `test_project_outline.cpp`. The shell itself branches only on `NoChange` (`Shell/LeftPane.cpp:205`). Everything the tools added since then has gone into `InvalidArgument` and `UnavailableOperation`, and the second became the catch-all for "it didn't happen". It cannot say "it partly happened". Three of the ten values never reach a model, and one (`UnsupportedSelection`) is never produced at all. The kind carries no details, so nothing machine-readable leaves the adapter except the settings and printer setup issue codes.
2. **Coordinator codes.** These grew one tool at a time. A few are designed and tested: `stale_workspace` for settings with details, `opened_before` with details, `feature_expired`, and `stale_revision`, which the page uses to draw a "stale" card. The rest are literal strings at the call site. The `invalid_argument` and `invalid_arguments` pair is an accident: the contract check uses the plural, and `workspace_error_code` uses the singular. Details are filled at eleven coordinator sites, all of them in the settings, printer setup and file-load paths: `:679`, `:732`, `:751`, `:763`, `:1038`, `:1084`, `:1909`, `:1927`, `:1958`, `:1969` and `:1974`. MCP adds details for the renamed stale codes, and the bridge adds `{reason}` for `connection_lost`. Every other failure sends `{}`.
3. **Settings issue codes.** This is the only designed contract, and the only one that meets criterion 1 ("changes nothing" is stated in the guide and holds in the code). It is documented in the tool guide's "Error codes" table, comes with correction details (suggestions, allowed values, bounds), and is tested in `tests/agent/test_tool_coordinator.cpp`. The guide and the code disagree in one place. The guide's table (line 858) says a requested object that is gone gives `workspace_unavailable`. The code gives `missing_object`, and the guide's own "Per-object overrides" section (line 1134) agrees with the code.
4. **Printer chat codes.** Not in the brief, but a fourth vocabulary. These are designed per surface, each message names the next step, they have 31 test assertions in `tests/agent/test_printer_conversation.cpp`, and three are named in the printer and filament instructions. They reach a model without details.

**What each kind of model actually reads.**

- **In-app model.** It reads the code, the message and the details (`AgentHost.cpp:2888-2889`), but nothing defines any code. The project prompt (`projectInstructions.ts`) says nothing about tool errors, and no skill does either. The printer and filament instructions name three codes: `unsupported_setting_mutation`, `read_only_preset` and `unknown_nozzle` (`printerInstructions.ts:56`, `:59`, `:97`; `filamentInstructions.ts:43-44`). Tool descriptions name five: `feature_expired`, `opened_before`, `unsupported_scope`, `not_selected` and `read_only_preset` (`ToolRegistry.cpp:956`, `:1057`, `:1102`, `:1342`). So the in-app model treats the code as an English word and acts on the message. Nothing at all tells it whether a failed call changed anything.
- **MCP client.** It reads the code, the message and the details, plus server instructions that define exactly two codes (`McpProtocol.cpp:184-187`). One of those definitions, `workspace_unavailable`, is wrong for the 40 renamed cases. The instructions also mention "preset revert", and no such tool exists.
- **Voice.** Messages are written in several voices: engineering ("Object ID belongs to an earlier project session", with no full stop), instruction to the model ("Read workspace_inspect again."), and instruction to the person ("Ask the Agent again.").

## 4. Recommendation

### 4.1 Verdict

Consolidate, in three stages, into one contract that meets all four criteria. Do not shrink everything into a small generic vocabulary. Instead:

- Keep one registered table in which every code has exactly one next-action class and a fixed set of details.
- Make every error state its outcome.
- Keep the specific codes that already teach well: the settings codes, the printer chat codes, `opened_before` and `feature_expired`.
- Split the generic kinds that span several classes.
- Spell each code the same way on both surfaces.
- Send impossible states to Sentry instead of to the model.

Doing only the minimal fixes would close today's known cases, but it leaves the cause in place. New tools would keep reaching for `UnavailableOperation` and literal strings, because nothing stops them. And no tool could report a half-finished change, because `CommandResult` has no way to say it.

### 4.2 The single contract

**Every error carries two fields beyond code and message.**

- `changed`: one of `none`, `partial`, `done` or `unknown`. This is criterion 1. The coordinator fills it as `none` for everything it refuses before `start_running`. The adapter must set it for failures after a change (Table E). For `partial`, the details name what was done; plate_layout, for example, can list the rows it applied.
- `next`: one of the six classes, F, R, W, P, A or S, spelled out as words. This is criterion 2. It comes from the code's entry in the table, so the call site cannot get it wrong.

Both fields are decisions for Kenneth (D2).

**Where it lives.** It goes in one header, `Agent/ToolErrors.hpp`, beside `ToolError` (`Agent/ToolExecution.hpp:49`). The header lists every code a model can receive, with its next-action class and the details keys it must carry. `fail()` takes an entry from that list, not a free string, so the compiler closes the set. The printer chat (`PrinterConversation.cpp`, `PrinterPanel.cpp`) and `ProviderAgent.cpp` use the same entries. The tool guide's "Error codes" section becomes the full table, states the four criteria, and points at the header.

This follows the repo rule that a rule lives next to what it governs. The meaning of a code lives with the code. The next step for one tool stays in that tool's message and description. No standing prompt text is needed, because each error explains itself.

**Adapter kinds.** The adapter is the only layer that knows whether OrcaSlicer was busy, refused, or failed, and whether it had already changed something. So the kind and the outcome have to be chosen at each failure site. The changes:

- Replace `UnavailableOperation` with `Busy` (W), `NeedsStep` (P), `Refused` (S) and `Failed` (S).
- Use `MissingObject`, renamed to `NotFound`, for every "that id is not in the open project", including the eight plate sites. Keep `StaleId` only for "belongs to an earlier session" and "was deleted since you read it".
- Delete `UnsupportedSelection`.
- Give `CommandResult` an outcome (`none`, `partial` or `done`) and an optional details JSON, so the adapter can say what it did and which id was not found.
- Where the order of steps allows it, check before changing, as the repo's error rules ask ("fix the ordering"). plate_layout's arrange and object_place's orient can claim the job worker before they change anything, so their "busy" can no longer arrive after a change.

**Invariants.** The cases in 3.9 throw instead of failing, the way `McpProtocol.cpp:243` and `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:3041` already do. In unit tests the product-state checks become test setup, not product code. The `stoull` overflow becomes part of the contract check, so it gets `invalid_arguments`.

**Code set reaching a model.** New or changed spellings are in bold.

| Class | Codes | Required details |
|---|---|---|
| F | `invalid_arguments` (absorbs `invalid_argument`), `unknown_tool`, `not_run`, the settings F codes, the printer chat F codes | the field or key when one is at fault |
| R | **`not_found`** (absorbs `invalid_id`, `missing_object` and the wrong-plate `stale_id`), `stale_workspace` (absorbs `stale_revision` and the remaining `stale_id`), `feature_expired`, `connection_lost` | `not_found`: `{kind, id, read}`, where `read` names the tool that lists valid ids. `stale_workspace`: expected and current session and revision, built in the coordinator for every stale case |
| W | **`busy`** | `{what}`; for slicing, `{preempt: true}`, since preempting is the person's decision to state |
| P | **`needs_step`** | `{tool}`, for example `slice_start` |
| A | `opened_before`, `workspace_unavailable` (only "no app, no project, or no FFF printer"), `withheld_setting`, `unsupported_setting_mutation`, the printer chat A codes | as today |
| S | **`refused`**, **`failed`**, `local_save_failed`, `cancelled` | `failed` and `refused`: OrcaSlicer's own text when there is any, and what was done when `changed` is `partial` |

`execution_failed` leaves the table: per criterion 4 it becomes a throw. The MCP fallback for a failed call with no error (`McpProtocol.cpp:248`) is itself an invariant case, and should throw too.

**How both adapters read it.**

- The coordinator maps an adapter kind to its entry in one function. That function replaces `workspace_error_code()`, the hand mapping at `:1760`, and the `StaleSettings` special cases.
- In-app, `tool_output_json` sends the entry unchanged.
- MCP's `activity_result` stops renaming codes: delete `McpProtocol.cpp:252-261`. The server instructions drop their two code sentences and say instead that every error's `changed` and `next` fields say what happened and what to do.
- Messages are rewritten in one voice, addressed to the model. Each one states the outcome when it is not `none`, and ends with the next action where there is one.

### 4.3 Cost

Stage 1 fixes truth and the worst wrong guidance, and is needed under every option; it is the list in 4.5. Stage 2 adds the header, the two fields, the outcome on `CommandResult`, the split kinds and the invariant throws, and moves the coordinator onto entries. Stage 3 rewrites the messages and the tool guide.

- **Source, about 20 files.**
  - `Workspace/Workspace.hpp`.
  - The five adapter files. That means about 95 call-site re-tags: 41 tool-reachable and 28 shell-only `UnavailableOperation` sites, 19 `StaleId`, 7 `InvalidId` and 6 `MissingObject`. The shell-only sites can become `Failed` or `Refused` mechanically, and the shell does not branch on them. On top of that, about 9 sites need an outcome and details (Table E), and two need their order changed. These are the only edits that need real thought.
  - `ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp`, about 60 `fail()` calls. `ToolRegistry.cpp:1800` and its id check. `ProviderAgent.cpp`. `PrinterConversation.cpp`, 22 sites. `PrinterPanel.cpp`. `AgentHost.cpp`.
  - `McpProtocol.cpp`, `McpRuntime.cpp` and `Bridge.cpp`. The bridge is a separate binary but can include the header.
  - `AgentUI/src/components/ToolActivityCard.tsx` and `TurnActivity.tsx`, which key on `stale_revision`.
- **Tests, about 12 files.**
  - Kind renames: `tests/jusprin_support/FakeWorkspace.hpp` (60 uses) and `FakeSettings.hpp` (8); `tests/workspace/test_workspace_contract.cpp` (16), `test_project_outline.cpp` (17) and `real_adapter_harness.cpp` (15); `tests/shell/shell_harness.cpp` (3). That is about 120 lines, mostly search and replace.
  - Code assertions: `test_tool_coordinator.cpp` (about 18 of its 32 code assertions change, mostly the eleven `invalid_argument` ones), `test_mcp_protocol.cpp` (3), `test_agent_bridge.cpp` (4), `test_provider_agent.cpp` (a few), and the page's card tests. The tests that construct a coordinator without a product state need one.
  - Unchanged: `test_printer_conversation.cpp` (31) and the Python bridge tests (7, all `workspace_unavailable` while the app is closed, which keeps its code).
  - New:
    - one test per next-action class on each surface;
    - one test proving that MCP no longer renames codes;
    - one test per Table E site that fails part-way through and checks `changed: partial` and what the details list;
    - one test that an invariant case throws.
- **Docs.** The tool guide's error sections.

### 4.4 What would break

- **MCP clients: none released.** I checked that `main` has no `Mcp/` folder, and that no tag contains `644f8bfaff`, the commit that added the bridge. Per the standing rule, a pre-release change needs no protocol version bump.
- **Saved projects.** `Agent/ProjectStateDocument.cpp:370` restores each activity's error code from a project's `current-state.json`. Chats saved before the change keep `stale_revision`, `unavailable_operation` and `invalid_argument`, and have no `changed` or `next` fields. The model reads these only as history, which is harmless. The page's stale card would stop recognising old `stale_revision` records unless it accepts both spellings.
- **Recorded prompt-harness requests** that contain tool errors will differ. That changes the recordings, not behaviour.
- **Unit tests that relied on the "This build cannot …" refusals** would now throw, which is the point. They need a product state in their setup.
- **The tool guide's standing sentence** "Native error codes and MCP error codes do not have to be spelled the same" (guide line 357) would be reversed. That is decision D3.

### 4.5 If Kenneth decides not to consolidate: the minimal fixes

These close every inconsistency this sweep found, in about 10 files and about 25 test lines. Fixes 1 to 5 are stage 1 of the recommendation.

1. Stop renaming `unavailable_operation` to `workspace_unavailable` (`McpProtocol.cpp:261`). Rewrite the server instruction so `workspace_unavailable` means only "the app is closed, or no project is open", and drop "preset revert". Add a test in `test_mcp_protocol.cpp`.
2. Change the eight "That plate is not in the open project" sites from `StaleId` to `MissingObject`, and use the same kind in `start_slice` (`:2156`, `:2159`). Make slice_report and slice_inspect fail with `missing_object` for an unknown plate instead of returning `valid: false`.
3. Make each Table E failure say what was already done. For example, plate_layout's could say "The layout was applied; the arrange did not start because OrcaSlicer is busy." Move the job-worker check in plate_layout and object_place ahead of the changes.
4. Change the `stale_revision` messages (`ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:943`, `:2074`) to "Nothing ran. Read the workspace again (preview again for a settings change), then call again." Change `unsupported_setting_mutation`'s "read-only" (`OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:3198`) to say that the tools do not change this setting and the person changes it in OrcaSlicer.
5. Change `local_save_failed`'s second message to "The change was made but could not be saved; do not repeat it." That message is at `:875` and `:883`; see also D5.
6. Map `InvalidArgument` to `invalid_arguments` (`:68`). Change the six literal calls and the printer setup issue at `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:1315`.
7. Make `id_error`'s message (`OrcaWorkspaceAdapter.cpp:2713`) end with "Read workspace_inspect for the current ids."
8. Make the printer setup `unknown_preset` (`:1272`) say that the printer is not installed, and that the person adds it from Home → Add printer.
9. Turn the invariant cases in 3.9 into throws.
10. Fix the guide's table row at line 858, where an object that is gone gives `missing_object`.

### 4.6 Decisions that are Kenneth's

**D1. Consolidate, or only patch.**

- (a) The full contract in three stages. Each failure says what happened and what to do next, on both surfaces, and new tools cannot add a vague code or hide a partial change. It costs about 20 source files and 12 test files, mostly mechanical. Old saved chats show old codes.
- (b) Only the minimal fixes in 4.5. These are cheap and ship in one small change. `UnavailableOperation` stays a catch-all, `CommandResult` still cannot say "partly", and the next tool can repeat both problems.
- (c) Stage 1 now, and the rest of the contract later. The false codes and the silent partial changes go away at once, and the bigger change waits for a quiet week.

My recommendation is (c) followed by (a). Stage 1 is the part that is actively harmful today.

**D2. Add `changed` and `next` fields to every error envelope.**

- (a) Both, on both surfaces. The error states its outcome and its next action, so no prompt or server instruction has to list codes. It costs about 25 tokens per error. The adapter has to report the outcome honestly at every site that fails after a change.
- (b) `changed` only. Criterion 1 is met in a machine-readable way. The next action is left to the code name and the message, so a client must know the table to act on the code.
- (c) Neither. State the outcome and the next step in the message text alone. This saves the tokens, and the in-app model already acts on message text. But nothing machine-readable says whether a retry is safe, and nothing forces a new tool to state the outcome.

I recommend (a). `changed` is the field that prevents double application, and it is the one criterion the current design cannot express at all.

**D3. One spelling on both surfaces.**

- (a) Same codes in-app and on MCP, with the MCP rename deleted. One table, one set of tests, and nothing can drift. This reverses the tool guide's current sentence.
- (b) Keep MCP-specific names, but rename into correct codes. The in-app codes can then change without affecting clients. You keep two tables, and the rename layer is exactly where today's worst false code comes from.

I recommend (a). No MCP client has been released, so this is the cheapest moment to choose it.

**D4. Should a busy OrcaSlicer make the tool wait instead of failing?** This applies to "busy with another job", "view not ready" and "presets not loaded".

- (a) Keep failing with `busy` and `changed: none`. The model decides, and nothing hangs. Models may also retry in a tight loop.
- (b) The coordinator holds the action until OrcaSlicer is free, up to a time limit. That means fewer errors and simpler model behaviour. A call can then take longer than a client's timeout, and a hold that never ends looks like a hang.

I recommend (a) now. Collect evidence in an eval before deciding on (b).

**D5. `local_save_failed` after the action ran.** Today the call is reported as failed even though its change happened (`ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp:875`, `:883`).

- (a) Keep it as a failure, with `changed: done` and a message that says "the change was made; do not repeat it". The person sees something went wrong, and with the outcome field the model can no longer mistake it for "nothing happened".
- (b) Report success, with a `saveFailed` warning in the result. The model knows the change happened. A save failure is then easier to overlook, and the repo's rule against turning a failure into success applies here.

I recommend (a). Under D2 the outcome field removes the double-application risk that made (b) tempting.

**D6. Partial changes: roll back, or report.** Table E lists failures after part of a change.

- (a) Report them truthfully with `changed: partial` and what was done, and leave the project as it is. This is simple and honest. The person or model may have to undo by hand, and project Undo does not reverse every part: dropped unsaved preset edits, for example, are not on the undo stack.
- (b) Roll back where an undo snapshot already brackets the change (plate_layout, project_delete_items, object_repair), so a failure means `changed: none`. This makes the outcome cleaner. But it drives OrcaSlicer's undo stack from inside a failing tool call, it leaves a redo step behind, and it cannot cover printer_setup's dropped edits.

I recommend (a), together with the reordering in 4.2. Reordering makes the most common partial cases impossible, and (a) keeps the rest honest.

### 4.7 What I did not verify

- Nothing was built or run. Every class and every "Changed?" value is my reading of the code around each `return`, not observed behaviour. The Table E rows are the ones most worth confirming with a fake-workspace test before relying on them.
- The "Not checked" outcomes: export write failures, project_open's "did not open", object_divide's "did not split", `cancelled` mid-job, and the printer chat's `add_failed` and `change_failed`.
- The slice_report `invalid_arguments` result from the live test is not reconciled with my reading (see 3.8).
- `OrcaReshape.cpp:297` ("The object list is not available") is unclassified.
- I did not check the HomeUI page or the Python probe (`tests/mcp/probe.py`) for code-dependent logic beyond grep, which found none in the probe.

content.text:
I reworked [tool-error-reporting-sweep.md](tool-error-reporting-sweep.md) around the four criteria. It is still untracked and not ignored, and no code changed. The biggest new finding came from checking criterion 1 ("did anything change"): nine places report a plain failure after part of the change has already happened, and none of them say so.

**What changed in the document**

- **Part 1 now opens with the yardstick.** It gives the four criteria in order and why each matters: truthful about what happened, then next action and who takes it, then consistency, then invariants. It also notes that the tool guide's own "Error codes" table meets none of the four.
- **Every inventory row has a "Changed?" column.** I filled it by reading the code before each failure's `return`. `ProjectStateTransaction` only batches change notifications and rolls nothing back.
- **The findings are organised by criterion:**
  - **Truth:** five codes or messages state something false, plus the partial-change cases (Table E).
  - **Next action:** the codes that cover more than one class, as before.
  - **Consistency:** the wrong plate id and wrong object id cases, as before.
  - **Invariants:** five impossible states reach the model as ordinary errors. `fail()` doesn't log or report to Sentry, so only the model ever sees them.

**New findings**

- **Failures after a partial change (Table E):**
  - `plate_layout` can apply the whole layout and then report "busy" because the arrange didn't start.
  - `object_place` can move the object and then report "busy" because auto-orient didn't start.
  - `printer_setup` drops unsaved preset edits before it tries to select anything, and can fail with the printer already switched.
  - `project_delete_items` and `object_repair` can fail midway through.
  - `CommandResult` has no way to say "partly", so the adapter couldn't report these even if it tried.
- **One more false message:** `unsupported_setting_mutation` says the setting is "read-only". It isn't; only the tools may not write it, and the person can change it in OrcaSlicer.
- **The "This build cannot …" and "Region annotations are not available here" errors only happen in unit tests.** Every `AgentHost` sets the product state they check for, and MCP calls go through the same host's coordinator.

**Changes to the recommendation**

- Every error would carry a `changed` field (`none`, `partial`, `done` or `unknown`) next to `next`.
- `plate_layout` and `object_place` would claim OrcaSlicer's background job runner before changing anything, so "busy" can no longer arrive after a change.
- The impossible states would throw instead of failing quietly, as two places already do.
- The minimal-fix list grew from 7 to 10 items.
- Decision 5 now favours keeping `local_save_failed` a failure with `changed: done`.
- A new decision 6 asks whether partial changes should be rolled back or reported. I recommend reporting them, plus the reordering above.

The "Changed?" values are my reading of the code, not observed behaviour. Table E is the part most worth confirming with a fake-workspace test before anyone relies on it. Used 2026-10-12 for the spiral vase investigation (branch `claude/spiral-vase-writable`).

**Recipe.** Start `build/arm64/tests/shell/Release/JusPrinShellHarness.app/Contents/MacOS/JusPrinShellHarness --manual-mcp <scratch dir>` with `HOME=<scratch home>`, wait for `HARNESS MCP FIXTURE READY` on stderr (about 15 s), read the URL from `<scratch dir>/jusprin/mcp.json`, then call tools with `probe.call(urlsplit(url), "tools/call", {"name": ..., "arguments": ...})` imported from `tests/mcp/probe.py`. The fixture is two plates, one 20 mm box each, Bambu X1C 0.4, "Bambu PLA Basic @BBL X1C", "0.20mm Standard @BBL X1C", the same presets as Kenneth's live tests. Another session's harness can run at the same time; the port falls back from 47301 and the discovery file is per data dir.

**Trap 1: leaked harness.** In a script, `cd "$S" && nohup harness ... &` makes `$!` the subshell, so `kill $!` leaves the harness running, and the next run's `rm -rf <fixture>` fails with "Directory not empty". Write `cd "$S"; nohup harness ... &`. Check with `pgrep -fl "<worktree>.*JusPrinShellHarness"` before finishing.

**Trap 2: slice_start on a sliced, unchanged plate.** The fixture's plate 1 starts sliced. `slice_start` on it (with or without `wait`) left it reported `sliced: false`, `slice_report` `valid: false`, and with `wait: true` the probe saw the stream close with no reply. Orca's log says "background process in idle state, use previous result". Change a setting first, then slice. Not investigated further.

**Timings on this Mac, Release config, load 30 to 40:** fresh worktree build of `jusprin_web jusprin_catalogs agent_bridge_tests workspace_contract_tests setting_display_tests shell_integration_harness` was 905 steps in about 14 min; the shell harness default regression (549 checks) about 2 min; the workspace adapter harness (972 checks) under 1 min. See [[jusprin-worktree-build]], [[live-test-built-app-on-mac]].

**Seeding a preset (2026-10-12).** `--manual-mcp` does not wipe its directory at start, so a user preset written to `<fixture>/user/default/machine/<name>.json` before launch (keys `from: User`, `inherits`, `name`, `printer_settings_id`, `version`, plus the values under test) is loaded and can be named as a settings `target.preset`. A Python driver that starts the harness with `subprocess.Popen` and terminates it in `finally` avoids Trap 1.


**Why a plate will not slice (2026-10-15).** MCP `slice_report` on a plate Orca refuses says only `valid: false`, with no reason even with `sections: ["findings"]`, and `slice_start` still answers `started: true`. Orca's own refusal text is in `<fixture>/log/debug_*.log`: grep `validate err=`. Used to reproduce the PETG HF on Smooth Cool Plate case (branch `claude/bed-type-mismatch`, worktree distracted-lehmann-9c1b12). See [[printer-setup-bed-type-check]].

**Slice waits, 2026-10-15 (jusprin-newui 336facf825).** Trap 2 re-measured: `slice_start {plateId, wait: true}` on the sliced, unchanged plate 1 got no reply in 120 s (a hang, follow-up task filed). Right after `printer_setup` fixes a plate Orca had refused, `slice_start` fails "That plate cannot be sliced as it stands" for about 3 s: the adapter checks `PartPlate::can_slice()`, whose invalid flag Orca refreshes only on its next deferred validation. A refused slice hanging the wait was fixed on branch `claude/slice-wait-refused` (worktree brave-panini-347b62): `WorkspaceSlicing::refused` carries Orca's ValidateError text. Over MCP every `unavailable_operation` reads as `workspace_unavailable` (McpProtocol.cpp), so don't take that code to mean JusPrin is closed.

name: pkill-cmake-build-leaves-ninja
description: "Builds on this shared Mac — one at a time, capped -j, never restart to change targets; the 2026-10-21 run that stacked 4 builds / 56 clangs on 12 cores"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 63cd6f14-4717-4149-ae93-daff41a73f76
  modified: 2026-10-21T19:12:06.265Z
---

On 2026-10-21 Kenneth found 4 Release builds and 56 clang processes on 12 cores, all mine, in one worktree. Every ninja ran at its default -j (cores + 2), so 4 × 14 = 56. He pointed out that the orphaned processes were the smaller problem. The bigger one was that I put that many builds there at all.

What I did wrong, in order of weight:
1. I treated builds as free on a machine other sessions build on too. I never passed `-j`. I saw load 33, then 76, and started more builds anyway.
2. I restarted the build three times to change its target list or to slip in a small target. Each restart cost a full set of jobs. Waiting for the running build and adding targets afterwards cost nothing.
3. I went against the brief ("reuse the existing build; another session may be building") by configuring a fresh full-app build for an optional live check.
4. I blamed the slowness on "other sessions" without counting my own processes. That is the plausible-story-instead-of-checking failure from CLAUDE.md.
5. Mechanism: `pkill -f "cmake --build <dir>"` kills only the wrapper. Its `ninja -C <dir>` child keeps compiling as an orphan. I never checked that a stop had worked.

**Why:** the machine is shared. My extra jobs slow every other session, and two ninjas in one build dir can leave its records inconsistent.

**How to apply:**
- Before starting a build, check `uptime` and `pgrep -fl ninja`. Cap jobs with `-- -j4` (fewer when load is above the core count).
- Decide the full target list once. Never restart a build to change it.
- Run one build per dir as its own process group (`set -m`, then kill with `kill -- -<pgid>`). After any stop, confirm with `pgrep -fl "ninja.*<dir>"`.
- Ask before a full-app build that the task did not require.

Related: [[background-bash-timeout-kills-builds]], [[track-wall-clock-on-background-work]], [[jusprin-worktree-build]].

On 2026-10-19 a side session cleaned up after a shell-harness run with `rm -rf /var/folders/*/*/T/jusprin-shell-*`, which also removed every other session's kept-for-inspection harness data dir (no harness was running at the time, so no live run broke).

Every new capability needs tests at each layer it passes through:

| Layer | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Registry | unique name, deterministic ordering, valid schemas, correct exposure and action class |
| Decoder | valid inputs, unknown fields, type errors, bounds, conflicting selectors |
| Fake workspace | success, expected failures, revision, events, atomicity, native undo/reset/revert and cancel semantics |
| Coordinator | stale session/revision, cancellation race, terminal result |

| OpenAI adapter | canonical schema projection and successful continuation |
| MCP adapter | canonical schema/output projection, bounded response, protocol errors, disconnect behavior |
| Shell/eval | real project and intended client complete the user task |

If a layer does not apply, say why in the PR. If something cannot be tested, state that openly as a limitation. It is not permission to leave out evidence without saying so.

The same run on the Windows verification machine, where the generator is Visual Studio and there is no `python3`:

```sh
cmake --build build --config Release --target OrcaSlicer agent_bridge_tests shell_integration_harness -- -m
build/tests/agent/Release/agent_bridge_tests.exe --order rand --warn NoAssertions
```

The workspace adapter harness also runs on that Windows machine, and passes (617 checks, exit 0, as of 2026-09-17). Put the app's `src\Release` on `PATH` first; otherwise the exe cannot load the `api-ms-win-crt` DLLs. In PowerShell, read the exit code with `$LASTEXITCODE`:

```powershell
$env:PATH = "$PWD\build\src\Release;$env:PATH"
build\tests\workspace\Release\workspace_adapter_integration_harness.exe
```

On 2026-09-16 it failed on Windows: `select_object(0)` returned false after `load_files`, seven checks failed, and the process died with `0xC0000005`. The test code was not stale. The cause was the machine setup. The Mesa provisioning script put `opengl32.dll` only in `mesa\`, where only the app launcher looks for it. A harness has no launcher, so this one ran on the system's GL 1.1 and its canvas never initialized. Selection is built from the canvas's volumes, so nothing could be selected, and the gizmo check then opened a paint gizmo with nothing selected. The script now also copies `opengl32.dll` beside each harness (see "Software GL on Windows machines without a GPU" in [engineering-method.md](engineering-method.md)); re-run it on existing build trees. With GL in place, two harness faults surfaced that only Windows shows:

- The move-event check asserted that the move was the last change. On Windows, queued `EVT_GLCANVAS_OBJECT_SELECT` events publish two Selection-only changes after it, so the check now skips those.
- The data-directory cleanup threw, because the open log file cannot be deleted, and the uncaught exception turned a PASS into `0xC0000409`. It now warns instead, as the shell harness already did.

Pulling the script change does not fix a build tree that was already provisioned; run the script on it again. So that a tree without GL cannot fail this way unnoticed again, the harness now checks, right after its first model load, that the canvas initialized GL. If it did not, the harness stops with `HARNESS ERROR the 3D canvas did not initialize OpenGL` and the command to fix it, exits 1, and does not crash. A clean exit on that early path also needed the harness to close the main frame, as the shell harness does. It used to call `ExitMainLoop()`, which skips `MainFrame::shutdown()`, and a pending project backup then posted to the deleted frame.

Node is required: the Agent and Home pages are built from TypeScript and their `index.html` is generated, not committed, so a tree without npm fails at configure time and an app built without them shows no Agent panel at all.

The Python bridge tests run there too, with the helper named explicitly, since the default path in `tests/mcp/test_bridge_process.py` is the macOS bundle:

```sh
JUSPRIN_TEST_BRIDGE=build/src/Release/jusprin-mcp.exe python -m unittest discover -s tests/mcp
```

That run is green as of 2026-09-16. It was not before. Eight live-peer tests failed on Windows — SSE progress, client cancellation, EOF with a pending call, stdout backpressure, the live catalog's header mirroring, and a malformed peer result — and the same eight failed from commits well before the M0 work, which is why they were first recorded here as an unexamined platform gap. Examining them found a single cause, and it was the helper's, not the tests': Windows hands `main()` its arguments and `getenv()` its values in the active code page, so `fs::u8path(argv[i])` could not spell the fixture's `discovery 打印.json`, `read_discovery` never found the file, every call fell back to the offline catalog, and nothing that needs a live peer could pass. The helper now takes anything that becomes a path from `CommandLineToArgvW` and `GetEnvironmentVariableW`; POSIX argv already carries the native bytes and is unchanged. The standing rule: in helper code a path may never arrive through a narrow Windows API, and the fixture's non-ASCII name earns its keep by catching exactly this.

Nothing else in the stdio contract differs on Windows — non-blocking stdout, SSE framing, cancellation and teardown all behave as the tests assume, including twenty consecutive runs of the blocked-stdout and backpressure cases. The same run also caught `tools/list` still asserting the pre-M0 catalog size, which the milestone updated in the C++ tests and not here. Run this suite on Windows for every milestone; a macOS pass is not evidence for it.

Catalog bytes per tool, the measurement every milestone PR reports, without `python3`. Run it with `pwsh`, not `powershell`: Windows PowerShell 5.1 cannot parse a catalog whose schemas nest as deep as this one's and reports **no tools at all** rather than an error, which looks exactly like a catalog that shrank to nothing. content.text:
I ran the Table E cases against the real tool code. Both cases that can be triggered from outside are confirmed: `plate_layout` returns a failure after earlier parts of the same call have already changed the project, and the error doesn't mention it. Four of the other Table E rows turn out to be unreachable, so the document's earlier "nine sites" was too high.

**Why not the fake workspace.** That was my suggestion, and it was wrong. The fake workspace replaces the OrcaSlicer adapter, which is exactly the code these failures live in, so it can't confirm them. I used the shell harness's `--manual-mcp` fixture instead. It runs the real adapter and the real MCP server, and I sent the tool calls from a short script.

**Which binary.** The harness in the main checkout (built 2026-10-20) wouldn't start. The current design-token file has a key it doesn't know, and the shell refuses to install without tokens. So I ran the harness built in worktree `zealous-hertz-f8d656` at `f073fdba96`, an ancestor of HEAD. Between that commit and HEAD, the files under test differ only in how the MCP client's name is recorded. I used that binary read-only with my own data folder, and changed nothing in the worktree. I built nothing.

**Results:**

- **Disabled object asked for copies:** confirmed. One call renamed object A, added a plate, disabled object B and asked for 3 copies of B. It failed with "OrcaSlicer did not change the copies of …". Afterwards A was renamed and the plate existed. A follow-up call asking only for copies of B was refused the same way, so B had stayed disabled. Re-enabling B in a later call let the copies through.
- **Plate limit:** confirmed. With 35 plates, a call adding 16 failed with "OrcaSlicer cannot add another plate" and left the project with 36.

the objects arrive, so the rule does not depend on which comes first. A
model dropped onto a project that already has objects is still logged as
